transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Avery Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (BlueShift), Carlos Perez (BlueShift), Lena Wu (BlueShift)

Summary:
- Deep dive on integrating Redwood telemetry with OpenTelemetry and existing observability stack.
- Focus on token-level metrics, spans for per-request and per-token operations, KV cache hit-rate, batching effects on latency, and how quantization affects observable signals.
- Action items: share OTEL collector configs, example dashboards, run benchmark on dedicated capacity to capture token-level latency and KV hit metrics.

Topics covered:
- OpenTelemetry spans and attributes for inference lifecycle
- Token-level metrics (per-token latency, emitter cost, kv cache hit/miss counters)
- Sampling and volume management (how to avoid exploding telemetry cost)
- Dashboards and SLOs (p50/p95/p99 token latency, batch size distribution, kv hit-rate)
- VPC/on-prem constraints for exporting telemetry and agentless collection
- How quantization and batching change latency distributions and observable markers

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for taking the time. we're gonna go deep on observability and otel integration today, especially around token-level metrics and how the runtime surfaces batching and kv cache behavior. can everyone see my screen?
[00:08] Maya: yep, can see. thanks, samir. we're most interested cause we're trying to tie token costs back to our billing and also build SLOs at the token level.
[00:14] Carlos: and we need this to feed into our existing datadog/grafana stack, so whatever you recommend should be easy to wire up to our otel collector.
[00:21] Avery: cool. quick intro: i'm avery, i work on runtime and instrumentation at redwood. i'll walk through suggested spans and metrics, then we'll map them to common exporters.
[00:29] Samir: quick note, transcription may have a couple typos for product names — you'll hear "Redwood Dedicate" and sometimes "KV cash" in the transcript, apologies.

[01:02] Avery: first, high level: we instrument at three levels: request-level spans (the whole inference call), stage-level spans (tokenization, compile/hot path, kv cache check, model forward, postprocess), and optionally token-level spans/metrics. request-level are cheap. token-level is high cardinality and can be heavy, so we do sampling and aggregation.
[01:32] Maya: token-level's exactly our concern — we want p95 per token for long responses. can you explain how batching affects that?
[01:40] Avery: sure. with batching, per-token latency isn't purely additive. suppose you have a batch of 8 requests and a single forward from the model for a group of tokens; the per-token time you measure includes queuing time while waiting to fill the batch. so you want metrics for batch size distribution and queue time. we emit attributes: redwood.batch.size, redwood.batch.queue_ms, and redwood.batch.exec_ms.
[02:01] Carlos: do you emit those as otel metrics or as span attributes?
[02:05] Avery: both options. span attributes are cheaper and attach to traces; we also export aggregated otel metrics for batch.size histogram and batch.queue_seconds histogram. for token-level, we emit counters and latency histograms labeled with model, deployment, and quantization profile — but we recommend sampling at like 1-5% by default to avoid telemetry explosion.

[02:40] Lena: how are kv cache hits recorded? we use a lot of prefix reuse, so hit-rate matters for cost.
[02:45] Avery: we instrument kv cache checks per request with a small set of metrics: redwood.kv.checks_total, redwood.kv.hits_total, and redwood.kv.hit_rate (derived). each check also emits a span event if miss happens for debugging. aggregate dashboards show hit-rate by model, sequence_length_bucket, and route.
[03:06] Maya: sequence length bucket? so you bucket tokens by prompt length?
[03:10] Avery: yes — we use coarse buckets (0-64, 65-256, 257-1024, 1025+) so cardinality stays manageable. we add sequence_length_bucket as a span attribute and metric label.

[04:00] Samir: can you walk us through the actual otel collector config you recommend? e.g., in our environment sending to datadog + s3 for raw traces.
[04:07] Avery: absolutely — the recommended pattern: send high-cardinality traces to a local otel collector with tail-sampling to pick interesting traces (errors, p99 latency, kv-miss heavy). export aggregated metrics (histograms/counters) to datadog/grafana, and S3 for long-term raw trace archival if you need for forensic. we'll share an example yaml.
[04:28] Carlos: question on tail-sampling — if we sample late, how do we keep token-level histograms accurate?
[04:33] Avery: good question. we separate concerns: token-level histograms are emitted as aggregated metrics from the runtime, so they don't require full trace data to be accurate. token-level spans/events are for debugging and are sampled. metrics are counters/histograms that are incremented in the hot path and exported at aggregation intervals.

[05:12] Maya: about costs — metrics at token-level sound expensive. how do you control rps of telemetry?
[05:17] Avery: we recommend a tiered approach: all deployments emit request-level metrics (throughput, p95,p99), batch histograms, and kv cache counters by default. token-level histograms are aggregated (e.g., per-deployment per-minute) and sampled. full token traces are sampled low. also offer rate-limiting in the collector and we can pre-aggregate on the node to reduce cardinality.

[06:00] Carlos: how do quantization choices surface in telemetry? we run int8 quantized models in prod and want to compare latency/cost vs float32.
[06:08] Avery: we add a quantization_profile label like redwood.quant.profile with values (fp32, fp16, int8, int4) and capture model.tflops or model.estimated_ops where available. dashboards can compare p50/p95 across profiles and show cost per 1k tokens. quantization often reduces exec_ms but can increase CPU pre/post work; we surface that with stage-level spans (dequantize_ms, kernel_exec_ms).

[07:00] Maya: any pitfalls to watch for on VPC or on-prem? we run in a locked-down VPC with egress via nat gateway.
[07:07] Samir: yeah, good point. telemetry exporters need egress. options: 1) run otel collector inside VPC and forward to your managed observability via proxy, 2) use agentless push via an internal metrics endpoint that we host inside the VPC when using private deployment, or 3) store raw traces in S3 within the VPC and allow secure transfer. we'll document network ports and firewall rules.

[07:45] Lena: from the SRE side, we want alerting rules. what thresholds do you recommend?
[07:51] Avery: typical SLOs: p95 request latency < X ms (depends on model and batch size), p99 per-token latency < Y ms for interactive use. for KV cache: alert when kv.hit_rate < 80% for a 5 minute window or when batch.queue_ms spikes above baseline. also alert on sudden increase in token variance (stddev) which often indicates change in prompt patterns or model change.

[08:30] Carlos: can we correlate business cost to telemetry? e.g., cost per 1k tokens broken down by route/company feature.

[08:36] Samir: yes we emit token counters by route and by organization id (if you tag requests). metric: redwood.tokens.total{route,my_route} and redwood.cost.estimated_per_1k{route}. estimate cost in the runtime with the model price table and export as a derived metric.

[09:05] Maya: what about cardinality explosion if we tag by org and prompt hash?

[09:10] Avery: avoid high-cardinality tags like raw prompt hash. use route, model_version, env, and coarse prompt classes (e.g., prompt_template_id). we support tokenized prompt template ids to give you correlation without raw text.

[10:00] Samir: demo time — avery, can you show the dashboard?
[10:04] Avery: sharing screen — here's a sample grafana dashboard: top row shows request throughput and error rate; second row shows batch size histogram and queue_ms heatmap; third row shows kv.hit_rate over time and token latency histograms split by quantization_profile; bottom has per-route cost. note the p95 spikes correspond to kv misses.
[10:35] Maya: nice — how do you instrument the KV miss events in the trace?
[10:39] Avery: for kv misses we emit a span event named "kv_miss" with attributes: key_length, seq_len_bucket, route, model. we also tag the parent span with kv_miss=true so you can filter traces.

[11:10] Carlos: for our Datadog export, can we keep the same metric names or do we have to translate?
[11:15] Avery: you can map them in the otel collector. we use standard otel metric names but prefix with redwood.*. collector translation rules can rename or add tags for datadog. we'll provide an example pipeline with datadog exporter and s3 exporter.

[12:00] Maya: you mentioned sequence_length buckets earlier. how does that interact with kv cache hit rate?
[12:05] Avery: short prompts tend to have higher reuse, so kv.hit_rate is usually higher in 0-64 bucket. we surface hit-rate by bucket so product teams can understand where cache helps. also sometimes quantization changes behavior because smaller mixed-precision kernels might change tokenization boundaries slightly — rare but observable.

[13:10] Lena: we run experiments with canary rollouts. can your tracing help compare candidates?
[13:16] Avery: yes — we add rollout tags to spans (rollout_id, variant) and produce comparative dashboards. you can run statistical tests on p95 or cost per 1k tokens across variants. we also support automatic regression alerts when a new rollout increases p99 by X% or reduces kv hit_rate.

[14:05] Carlos: practical question — if we want token-level histograms per-minute, what's the cardinality and storage cost?
[14:12] Avery: sample calculation: if you have 10k rps and you emit per-deployment per-minute histograms with labels (model, quant_profile, route, bucket) that's maybe a few hundred unique series per minute — ok. but if you try to tag by user/org+route+prompt_template you'll multiply. recommended: keep per-minute rollups at deployment+model+quant_profile+route. raw token traces should be sampled low and archived if needed.

[15:20] Maya: can we get some recommended Grafana panels and alert examples?
[15:24] Samir: yes, samir to share dashboard json. we'll include panels for: request latency heatmap, token latency histogram, batch size distribution, kv.hit_rate sparkline, cost per 1k tokens, tail-sampled trace list for p99 events.

[16:00] Avery: also worth noting we expose internal runtime debug counters behind a flag — these include kernel stall counts, memcopy_ms, and kv_eviction_rate. those are off by default but useful for deep perf debugging.

[16:40] Carlos: about private deployment — how does telemetry flow? we use Redwood Private inside our VPC.

[16:46] Samir: for Private we can deploy an OTEL sidecar with the inference nodes or run a centralized collector in your logging subnet. you control where metrics go; we just emit to the local collector endpoint. for added security, we support mutual TLS between nodes and collector and can integrate with your KMS for credential rotation.

[17:30] Lena: any special considerations for on-prem GPU boxes? network bandwidth to exporters could be an issue.

[17:36] Avery: yes keep telemetry sampling low on constrained networks, do local aggregation, and ship compressed batches. we can also configure the collector to persist to disk during network outages and forward when healthy.

[18:00] Maya: let's talk about specific metric names. can you list the top 10 we should expect?
[18:05] Avery: sure: redwood.requests.count, redwood.requests.duration_ms (histogram), redwood.batch.size (histogram), redwood.batch.queue_ms (histogram), redwood.batch.exec_ms (histogram), redwood.kv.checks_total, redwood.kv.hits_total, redwood.token.latency_ms (histogram, sampled/aggregated), redwood.tokens.total (counter), redwood.quant.profile (label).

[19:00] Carlos: how do we avoid double counting tokens when we have retries and fallbacks?

[19:05] Avery: we attach a request_id and attempt_id attributes. tokens are counted per attempt but you can deduplicate in downstream by considering only final_attempt=true or by correlating attempt_id. we emit redwood.request.attempt=1,2 etc.

[20:00] Maya: on accuracy — when we roll quantized models we sometimes see subtle output regressions. can we tie quality metrics into this telemetry?
[20:07] Avery: yes, we support hooking evals into the pipeline: you can emit redwood.quality.regression_count when an eval prompt set fails thresholds. link those alerts to rollouts so the SRE and ML teams see quality and perf regressions together.

[21:15] Carlos: interesting. for our immediate next step we want a benchmark on a dedicated pool to capture token latency, batch distribution, and kv hit rate under our prompt set. how do we start?
[21:22] Avery: we'll provide a benchmark harness that runs your prompt set with configurable concurrency and streaming enabled. it will output otel metrics and a csv of per-request timings. run it in a dedicated pool (we can spin a trial) so we isolate from noisy neighbors.

[22:10] Maya: if we enable streaming, does that change telemetry? we often stream tokens to UI.
[22:15] Avery: streaming adds per-token emission points; we emit token send latencies and socket/transport metrics. streaming also reduces perceived latency for users but may increase total work due to smaller internal batches — we'll show this in the batch.size distribution panel.

[23:00] Lena: are there built-in annotations for model version changes to correlate with sudden shifts?
[23:05] Avery: yes every trace and metric includes model_checksum and model_version attributes so you can filter by version. we also recommend tagging deploy_id and rollout_id.

[24:10] Samir: let's cover security: does exporting telemetry leak prompt text?
[24:16] Avery: by default we do not export raw prompts. raw text is redacted from spans and only a prompt_template_id or prompt_token_count is exported. if you opt-in to raw text for debugging we can encrypt it in transit and at rest; for private deployments you can keep that data inside your VPC.

[25:00] Carlos: any gotchas with datadog tags? datadog has a tag cardinality model we need to respect.
[25:06] Avery: map high-cardinality attributes to low-cardinality labels and use datadog's tag remapping. avoid using user_id or raw prompt slices as tags. use route and prompt_template_id instead.

[26:00] Maya: i want to see an example trace for a p99 event. can you show one?
[26:05] Avery: sure — here's a trace with spans: request start -> tokenization (20ms) -> kv_check (5ms, miss) -> model forward (120ms) -> postprocess (15ms). note the kv_miss event at the kv_check span; that correlates with a batch.queue_ms spike earlier.

[27:10] Carlos: when we compare float and int8 profiles do you include memory metrics? sometimes int8 uses less GPU memory and changes eviction behavior.

[27:15] Avery: we emit memory.used_bytes and eviction_count as metrics when the internal debug flag is enabled. those go to the infra dashboard.

[28:00] Maya: let's capture an example alert: if kv.hit_rate drops 20% in 5 mins and p95 increases by 30% then page oncall and create an incident ticket.

[28:08] Samir: we'll include that as an example rule in the dashboard json we share.

[29:00] Carlos: latency distribution sometimes shows a bimodal pattern. does that map to batched vs unbatched requests?

[29:05] Avery: yes — unbatched (single-request) flows show lower queue_ms but can have higher exec_ms per token. we add a label batched=true/false to traces to let you split the histogram. the dashboard has a stacked histogram to reveal that.

[30:10] Maya: any recommendations for storage retention? how long to keep raw traces vs aggregated metrics?
[30:16] Avery: typical pattern: keep aggregated metrics (prometheus histograms/OTEL metrics) for 90 days; keep raw tail-sampled traces for 30 days; archive to S3 for 1 year if needed for audits. depends on your compliance needs.

[31:00] Carlos: can we get a sample collector config now?

[31:05] Avery: yes we'll email a yaml. it will show exporters for datadog and s3, a processor to drop high-cardinality attributes, and tail-sampling rules to capture errors and high-latency traces.

[32:00] Maya: in private deployment mode, how do RBAC and audit logs work for telemetry?

[32:06] Samir: telemetry access is gated by RBAC in the console; audit logs capture who downloaded dashboards, who changed alert rules, etc. for private deployments we can forward those logs to your SIEM.

[33:00] Lena: when we run perf debugging with Redwood engineers, what level of instrumentation will you enable?

[33:06] Avery: with permission we enable internal debug counters and can do live kernel-level traces. this is typically done for POC/perf tuning and requires a short maintenance window.

[34:10] Samir: question for blue shift — what's the target p95 and cost per 1k tokens you're aiming for?

[34:16] Maya: p95 interactive around 400ms for our chat UI, and cost ideally < $0.15 per 1k tokens. those are targets, subject to adjustments when we test with quantized models.

[34:45] Avery: good targets. we'll show how to map your SLOs into alert rules and synthetic checks.

[35:30] Carlos: our network team needs the exact port list and TLS fingerprint for the collector.

[35:35] Samir: we'll add that to the VPC docs we send.

[36:10] Maya: if we want to sample more aggressively for certain routes, can we do route-based sampling?

[36:16] Avery: yes — the collector supports conditional sampling by route, model, or rollout_id. that way you can collect more traces for high-value routes without increasing global telemetry.

[37:00] Lena: curious about the quantization telemetry — will you show how kernel exec time differs between int8 and fp16?

[37:06] Avery: yes — stage-level spans include kernel_exec_ms and dequantize_ms; comparing those across quant_profile gives you a breakdown. often you'll see lower kernel_exec_ms but slightly higher dequantize_ms for int8.

[38:10] Carlos: for the benchmark harness, can it emit OTEL metrics natively? we want the test results to flow into our dashboards automatically.

[38:16] Avery: yes the harness emits OTEL metrics and can be configured to target your collector endpoint. it will also produce CSV artifacts if you want to do local analysis.

[39:00] Maya: ok wrap-up — what are the concrete next steps?

[39:05] Samir: recap: 1) Samir sends OTEL collector yaml and grafana dashboard json; 2) Avery provides benchmark harness and runs a trial dedicated pool; 3) BlueShift provides prompt set and SLOs; 4) Carlos confirms VPC/firewall.

[39:30] Maya: sounds good. we'll aim to have prompt set by Fri.

[40:00] Carlos: one last Q on billing — can you tag metrics so we can allocate cost per product line?

[40:05] Avery: yes add route and product_tag as request labels and we'll emit cost metrics with those labels. again, keep cardinality low.

[41:00] Lena: for incidents, can traces auto-link to support tickets?

[41:06] Samir: yes our console can create a permalink to the trace and we can push that into your incident system via webhook.

[42:00] Maya: thanks, this was helpful.

[42:04] Samir: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[42:30] (meeting winds down; participants confirm next steps and end call)

End of transcript.
